summary: Redwood AE+SE gave an Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations to reduce per-token cost while meeting NimblePay latency SLOs. Discussed tradeoffs (latency vs cost), caching warmup, TTLs, hit rates, model variant fallbacks, and a proposed pilot to run benchmarks with NimblePay's traffic profile. Action items: pricing spreadsheet, perf scripts, and traffic/prompt share.
transcript:
[00:00] Laura Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Laura from Redwood, and Miguel is here from our SE team. Good to see you all.
[00:07] Sarah Patel: Hi Laura, hi Miguel, thanks. We wanted today to see concrete recommendations — our CFO keeps asking about cost per 1M requests — and Omar is here to make sure the infra side is feasible.
[00:17] Miguel Torres: Great, we'll walk through Optimize — the batching and caching guidance — and show a small demo. Quick note, sometimes the auto-transcript calls our product "RedWood Optimize" or "Redwoods Optimize" but it's Redwood Optimize.
[00:27] Omar Reyes: haha noted. We'll also want to understand VPC/private constraints.
[00:31] Miguel Torres: Totally. Quick agenda: 1) batching basics and tradeoffs, 2) prefix / KV cache patterns, 3) cost model and worked examples, 4) pilot ask.
[00:40] David Kim: Sounds good. We run a mixture of short transactional prompts (balance checks, auth) and long generation for statements. Latency SLO for transactional is 150-200ms p50.
[00:52] Miguel Torres: Ok that's helpful. So batching helps throughput and unit cost by aggregating tokens across multiple concurrent requests, but it can add queuing latency. We typically recommend adaptive batching with latency buckets — small latency targets keep the batch windows tiny. Example: if target p95 is 200ms, we limit batching wait to 15-25ms and rely on immediate dispatch for singletons. Note: adaptive batching is in the Optimize console as a suggestion.
[01:16] Sarah Patel: Can you show numbers?
[01:19] Miguel Torres: Sure. Example baseline: single-request throughput no batching — 1 token cost X. With batching of 8 requests average, per-token compute utilization improves by ~3.2x — rough. In practice in Redwood's internal tests we saw cost per token drop 25-40% at moderate batch sizes. But that varies by sequence length distribution.
[01:43] Laura Chen: I'll drop a spreadsheet after — sample calc that converts token/sec to GPU-hours and then to $/1M tokens with and without batching.
[01:50] David Kim: When you say sequence length distribution, we have many short prompts — 20-40 tokens — and a small tail that is 600-1000 tokens.
[01:59] Miguel Torres: That's a classic mix. Batching helps you on the short prompts because you can pack many in a single forward pass. For long tail, batching is less effective and we often recommend a split: route long sequences to dedicated instances (or use per-request path w/ smaller batch windows).
[02:13] Omar Reyes: And how does caching fit in?
[02:15] Miguel Torres: Two layers: prefix caching (common prefixes across requests) and KV cache (key-value based cached past KV cache states for continuation). Prefix cache works great for things like repetitive system prompts or templates — you avoid recomputing the first N tokens. KV cache is used for resumed generation where you serve the cached KV states for previously seen prefixes to skip early attention work. Both reduce tokens processed and latency for subsequent calls.
[02:42] Sarah Patel: Are those caches persistent across sessions?
[02:45] Miguel Torres: Yes, KV cache can be stored in a cold store and warmed into GPU memory when a request matches; prefix cache is typically in a fast in-memory store and has TTLs. There's a tradeoff: more persistent caching improves hit rates but increases storage and warmup complexity.
[02:59] David Kim: Can you quantify hit rates needed for meaningful savings?
[03:03] Miguel Torres: Rough rule of thumb: at 30-40% effective hit rate on prefixes you start to see noticeable cost reduction; at 60%+ you get major wins. But depends on the length of the prefix you're saving (if prefix is 50 tokens vs 5 tokens). We'll run your prompt set against the cache simulator to estimate.
[03:22] Laura Chen: We also want to call out cold-starts — first request will still pay full compute. We factor cache warmup into pilot expectations.
[03:29] Omar Reyes: For persistent KV cache, do you have KMS/HSM considerations? We need encryption at rest.
[03:34] Miguel Torres: Yes — in Private deployments or Dedicated we support KMS integration; cache blobs can be encrypted at rest and we store access logs. For the hosted flow we have envelope encryption and audit logs; I'll attach the security docs.
[03:46] Sarah Patel: Nice. Let's go into the cost model you mentioned.
[03:49] Miguel Torres: I'll share a concrete worked example. Suppose you have 1M transactions/day, average 30 tokens request + 10 tokens response = 40 tokens roundtrip. Without batching cost per 1M tokens is C1 (we'll show exact numbers in the spreadsheet). With batching and a 35% cache hit on 10-token prefixes, effective token compute drops — you only process new tokens for cache misses. Also batching moves you to better GPU utilization which reduces the per-token GPU-hour.
[04:20] Miguel Torres: Quick math: baseline compute tokens = 40M tokens/day. If prefix cache saves 10 tokens on 35% of requests, you're saving 3.5M tokens/day => 8.75% reduction. If batching gives another 30% efficiency, combined you can approach ~35-40% total cost reduction. (These are illustrative, we'll simulate with your actual traffic).
[04:46] David Kim: Those sound plausible. We care most about p95 latency for auth endpoints. Will batching break p95?
[04:53] Miguel Torres: It's where the tuning matters — adaptive batching respects per-route latency SLOs. You can set per-route batch windows and absolute latency budgets. We also support hybrid routing: critical auth route is served on a low-latency pool with minimal batching while bulk routes go to higher-batch pools for cost efficiency.
[05:10] Laura Chen: In the console you can set route-level policies — route -> model variant -> batch profile -> cache TTL. We can demo the console after slides.
[05:20] Miguel Torres: One implementation note: we have continuous KV cache eviction heuristics to avoid memory blowup — LRU-ish with telemetry. There's also a cold-store warming pipeline when a cached key is evicted and re-requested frequently.
[05:34] Omar Reyes: What's the expected CPU/RAM cost to host the cache? If we run private, we need to size boxes.
[05:40] Miguel Torres: For prefix cache in-memory you can expect small footprint per entry — if you save up to 100k prefixes across your tenant that's maybe a few GBs; KV cache entries are larger because they store KV tensors — those are usually the dominating factor and we recommend storing KV blobs in an object store and warming to GPU memory on demand. We'll provide recommended sizing for your pilot based on prompt lengths.
[06:01] Sarah Patel: Can we see the console demo now?
[06:04] Miguel Torres: Yes, demoing live console — sharing my screen now... (audio: 6s of UI noise)
[06:15] Miguel Torres: Here is the Optimize page. On the left, batch profiles — you can create a profile with max batch size, max latency wait ms, and priority buckets. I'll click a sample profile "fast-auth" — max batch 4, wait 15ms. Notice the simulation graph shows expected latency distribution and cost impact.
[06:36] Sarah Patel: That simulation — where does the data come from?
[06:39] Miguel Torres: It uses your uploaded traffic histogram. If you don't upload, we run default distributions. For the pilot we'll ingest your 24h sample to make it accurate.
[06:47] Laura Chen: Also, here is prefix cache config — you can set TTLs, prefix normalization rules (strip session ids), and an estimated hit rate preview from the simulator. Notice the "warm pool" checkbox which keeps hot keys preloaded.
[06:59] David Kim: The normalization rules are key for us because our prompts have PCI tokens in them we need to strip.
[07:05] Miguel Torres: Right — we recommend normalization + hashing to avoid storing PII. Also support for token scrubbing before caching.
[07:12] Omar Reyes: How do you measure cache hits for billing? Do hits reduce billed tokens?
[07:17] Miguel Torres: Billing is based on tokens processed by the runtime. If prefix cache avoids computing N tokens, those tokens are not billed. We report token counts and cost savings in the Console and via the billing export.
[07:29] Sarah Patel: Can you explain KV cache warmup latency — if we hit a warmup, will auth be impacted?
[07:34] Miguel Torres: If a KV blob needs to be loaded from object store to GPU, there's a warmup penalty (tens to a few hundreds of ms depending on size and infra). That's why we recommend hybrid strategies: keep auth on low-latency pool (small batch, minimal cache warmup) and let high-throughput features benefit from longer tail caching.
[07:52] David Kim: For the pilot, we'd like to target our auth route and our statement gen route separately.
[07:57] Laura Chen: That aligns with our recommended pilot: 1) ingest 24h traffic, 2) create routes/profiles for auth vs batch jobs, 3) run 48-72h benchmark comparing baseline vs optimized. Miguel will run the perf harness with your tokens.
[08:12] Miguel Torres: We'll also test fallbacks — for instance, if Dedicated pool is busy we can route to a cheaper model variant with automatic quality regression alerts. That avoids 503s.
[08:22] Sarah Patel: Competitors like OpenAI — do you have direct cost comparisons?
[08:26] Laura Chen: We maintain apples-to-apples comparatives using equivalent open models and our runtime optimizations. We'll include a slide with example modeled costs vs a generic hosted API — but every workload differs so pilot is the best source.
[08:40] Omar Reyes: Security one more time: SSO/SCIM, audit logs, and KMS — can we get the SOC2 and network diagrams?
[08:48] Laura Chen: Absolutely — I'll share SOC2 and a private deployment network diagram pack.
[08:52] Miguel Torres: One more technical note on batching: we support per-model kernels and quantization profiles that affect how much benefit batching yields. Some 4-bit quantized kernels have different parallelization behaviors. We'll recommend model variants per workload.
[09:06] David Kim: Good. For our numbers — can you run the simulator with our traffic and a hypothetical 10k RPS peak?
[09:12] Miguel Torres: Yes, please send the traffic histogram and top prompts and we'll run the simulator overnight. We'll include results as part of the pricing calc.
[09:19] Sarah Patel: Regarding metrics — what telemetry will we get during pilot?
[09:23] Miguel Torres: Console provides per-route token counts, batch sizes, cache hit rates, latency percentiles, and cost breakdown by model/pool. We also provide traces for individual requests.
[09:34] Laura Chen: Recap and next steps — Laura to send pricing + security docs, Miguel to prepare perf harness and schedule pilot run, NimblePay to share traffic and prompts. Target pilot week of 2025-05-26. Any final questions?
[09:48] Omar Reyes: No, that is good. I'll talk to procurement about the Dedicated capacity options.
[09:52] Sarah Patel: Thanks everyone.
[09:54] Miguel Torres: Thanks all — we'll follow up via email with artifacts and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[09:59] (call ends)

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mis-IDs ("Redwood Optimize" vs "Redwood's Optimize"), filled pauses removed in some places, and UI demo audio clipped. Pilot proposal (short):
- Ingest: NimblePay provides 24h anonymized traffic + top-100 prompts.
- Config: two route profiles (auth: low-latency, statement-gen: high-batch + prefix/KV cache).
- Run: 48-72h A/B test baseline vs optimized with telemetry export.
- Deliverable: cost delta, latency p50/p95/p99, cache hit rates, and recommended production config.

End of transcript.
